Denise, thanks for making the time. I am writing the regional leadership profiles and I would rather hear it from you than from the org chart.
Happy to. I spearhead commercial operations across Latin America, and I oversee a cross-functional team of forty.
And where does your scope stop? That is the part the org chart never shows.
Anything above the local limits I liaise with Milan on. Below that, the accountability is mine. I have three counterparts in the region and we set the priorities together.
You came from the technical side, is that right? Most people in your seat came from sales.
I did. And honestly, if I had stayed there, I would never have built the broker network. That network is what drove the region last year.
That is the line I was looking for. What is the hardest part of the job right now?
Alignment. Four countries, four markets, and every stakeholder reads the same number differently. Getting to one set of deliverables takes longer than producing them.
I will use that. And I will use it in your words, not mine.

The hardest part of the job is alignment.

I have listened to something like three thousand senior introductions, and almost all of the weak ones make the same two mistakes. The first is listing tasks. People tell me everything they do in a week, and by the fourth item I have lost the shape of the job. A list is not a scope. The second is starting with an apology, and it is nearly always about English. Nobody in the room was going to think about your accent until you pointed at it. And here is something people find hard to hear. The size of your team is the least interesting number you can give me. Forty people, four hundred people, it tells me almost nothing. What decisions do you make that nobody above you reviews? That is the real question. So I ask everyone the same thing now. In one sentence: what breaks if you leave tomorrow? If you can answer that, you can introduce yourself anywhere.

Twelve years ago I turned down a job I still think about. It was a bigger title at head office, a team of two hundred, and a much shorter commute. I took a smaller role instead, running one market, with real accountability for the number. My mother thought I had lost my mind. If I had taken the head office job, I would have had a wonderful title and almost no decisions. And I would not have learned the thing that actually made my career, which is how to lose money, and how to explain losing it to a board without losing the room. Nobody teaches that. You only learn it when the number is yours. One piece of advice about telling this story. Tell it as judgement, not as luck. Say what you chose and why you chose it. If you tell it as something that happened to you, people hear a passenger. If you tell it as a decision, they hear a director.

I spearhead commercial operations across Latin America for an Italian insurance group. I oversee a cross-functional team of forty and I liaise with Milan above the local limits. Below those limits, the accountability for the region is mine. If I had stayed on the technical side, I would never have built the broker network.
